query: For an elemental Cr coating on a zirconium-alloy fuel-cladding substrate, what single intervention could prevent premature coating failure caused by elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion while preserving protection under both normal subcritical-water operation and accident-relevant high-temperature steam? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism, predicts performance relative to the unmodified Cr-coated baseline, defines the relevant temperature, exposure-time, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a discriminating experiment and outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a thin, aluminum‐rich diffusion barrier interlayer between the zirconium‐alloy substrate and the elemental Cr coating will suppress the high‐temperature interdiffusion of Cr and Zr by forming a stable, dense alumina scale that impedes atomic migration, thereby preventing premature coating failure while maintaining the protective function under both normal subcritical-water conditions and accident-relevant high-temperature steam.
generation.material_initial_state: A zirconium-alloy fuel-cladding substrate with an elemental Cr coating that currently exhibits premature failure due to elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin aluminum-rich barrier layer (for example, via physical vapor deposition) onto the zirconium-alloy substrate just prior to applying the elemental Cr coating.
generation.conditions: The samples would be evaluated under simulated pressurized water reactor (PWR) primary water conditions (subcritical water conditions) and under high-temperature steam conditions representative of accident scenarios (with exposure durations typical for each state). Temperature and time are controlled variables as defined by reactor operating standards and accident simulation protocols.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, dense Al2O3 (alumina) scale within the interlayer that serves as an effective barrier to atomic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the aluminum-rich interlayer oxidizes to form a stable alumina scale that physically and chemically limits the interdiffusion of Cr and Zr. This reduces the formation of brittle intermetallic phases and preserves the integrity and adhesion of the Cr coating under both normal operating temperatures and the transient high temperatures encountered during accidents.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified Cr-coated baseline, the modified system is predicted to exhibit a significantly reduced interdiffusion zone and improved coating adhesion, leading to enhanced overall oxidation and corrosion resistance. The exact magnitude of improvement is uncertain and will need experimental quantification.
generation.baseline: Elemental Cr coating on zirconium-alloy fuel-cladding which fails prematurely due to significant Cr–Zr interdiffusion at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Performance is assessed under conditions matching normal PWR subcritical-water operation and accident-relevant high-temperature steam exposures, with exposure durations appropriate to each regime.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal thickness and specific composition of the Al-rich barrier for maximal diffusion suppression are not predetermined, and the quantitative reduction in interdiffusion remains to be measured.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set with the standard elemental Cr coating and a second set with an added thin aluminum-rich barrier interlayer deposited between the zirconium-alloy substrate and the Cr coating. Subject both sets to cyclic exposure tests under simulated subcritical water conditions and high-temperature steam conditions. After testing, perform cross-sectional microscopy and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to assess the width of the Cr–Zr interdiffusion zone and to evaluate coating adhesion and oxidation products.
measurements: Thickness of the interdiffusion zone via EDS mapping
Coating adhesion quality (via scratch tests or pull-off tests)
Oxidation weight gain and scale integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the Al-rich barrier do not show a measurable reduction in the Cr–Zr interdiffusion zone or improved coating adhesion/oxidation resistance compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The TaO and ZrO2 passivated films were formed from +Ta and +Zr coatings during the corrosion process, and Cr2O3 showed better corrosion resistance. Due to the presence of highly electronegative components, RHEAs have a strong ability to regenerate passivated films in surface defects. The electronegativity values of Ti, Mo, Nb, Ta, Cr and Zr are about 1.54, 2.61, 1.60, 1.50, 1.66 and 1.33, respectively, and these can easily obtain electrons []. As the metal’s electronegativity increases, the electronegativity difference between the oxygen and metal decreases. Elements obey the acid–base rule, and protect the underlying metal by replicating an oxide layer to slow down the corrosion process. Cr has greater electronegativity than Ta and Zr, so it has a greater ability to regenerate passivation films. In the process of preparing a refractory high-entropy alloy coating, elements in the substrate diffuse to the coating due to the high temperature, and a small amount of Al is present in the coating. We report multi-component high-entropy materials as extraordinarily robust diffusion barriers and clarify the highly suppressed interdiffusion kinetics in the multi-component materials from structural and thermodynamic perspectives. The failures of six alloy barriers with different numbers of elements, from unitary Ti to senary TiTaCrZrAlRu, against the interdiffusion of Cu and Si were characterized, and experimental results indicated that, with more elements incorporated, the failure temperature of the barriers increased from 550 to 900°C. The activation energy of Cu diffusion through the alloy barriers was determined to increase from 110 to 163 kJ/mole. Mechanistic analyses suggest that, structurally, severe lattice distortion strains and a high packing density caused by different atom sizes, and, thermodynamically, a strengthened cohesion provide a total increase of 55 kJ/mole in the activation energy of substitutional Cu diffusion, and are believed to be the dominant factors of suppressed interdiffusion kinetics through the multi-component barrier materials.
